h1: Criminal Record Expungement (Expunction) Lawyer El Paso, TX
intro: A dismissed case still shows up on a background check until a court orders it erased. Attorney Robert Navar files expunction petitions in El Paso County district court so the arrest, the charge and the booking record are destroyed — not just hidden.
summaryHeading: Dismissed is not the same as erased
summary: An expunction under Chapter 55A of the Texas Code of Criminal Procedure (formerly Chapter 55) orders the agencies that hold a record of your arrest or charge to destroy it, and in general lets you lawfully deny the arrest.

You may qualify if the case was dismissed, you were acquitted, a grand jury no-billed it, or you completed deferred disposition on a Class C misdemeanor. Some arrests that never led to a charge qualify after a waiting period.
The petition is filed in El Paso County district court at 500 E. San Antonio Ave; how long it takes depends on the court's docket and the agencies' responses.
We confirm eligibility against the current statute before filing and quote a flat fee after a free consultation. Call 915-503-1600 or schedule an appointment.

sections.heading: Expunge vs. Seal: What an Order of Expunction Does
paragraphs: People use "expunge" and "seal" as if they were the same thing. In Texas they are not. An order of expunction directs every agency named in the order — police, sheriff, DPS, the prosecutor, the court clerk — to return or destroy the records of the arrest and charge. Once the order is final, you may in general deny the arrest on job applications and most forms. The main exception is a later criminal proceeding where the expunged matter itself is at issue, and some federal forms have their own disclosure rules.

An order of nondisclosure, by contrast, seals the record from the public and from private background-check companies but leaves it visible to law enforcement, licensing boards and certain state agencies. Expunction is the stronger remedy, and it is the one many of our former ticket clients qualify for, because a Class C case that ended in dismissal is generally expungeable.

Expunction does not reach everything. A case that ended in a conviction is generally not expungeable, and a record already sealed by nondisclosure does not automatically become expungeable later. We check both paths against your actual court history before recommending one.

sections.heading: The Outcomes That Generally Qualify
paragraphs: The expunction chapter lists the situations in which a person is entitled to an expunction. The ones we see most often in El Paso are below. Eligibility rules change — the chapter was renumbered as Chapter 55A effective January 1, 2025 — so we confirm your facts against the current statute before anything is filed.

list.text: the charge was dismissed and, in general, either the limitations period has run or the dismissal was for a reason the statute recognizes, such as mistake or false information.
you went to trial and were found not guilty, or were convicted and later pardoned or found actually innocent.
the grand jury declined to indict and the applicable waiting period has passed.

the ticket or other Class C charge was dismissed after you finished deferred disposition under art. 45A.302. Expunction of a Class C charge is available under art. 55A.051 because the bar for court-ordered community supervision does not apply to Class C misdemeanors; these are generally eligible once the deferral is completed and the dismissal entered.
an arrest that never produced a charge may be expunged after a waiting period that depends on the offense level, or sooner if the prosecutor certifies the records are no longer needed.

sections.heading: Filing in El Paso County District Court: Petition, Agencies, Hearing
paragraphs: We start by pulling the real record: your DPS criminal history, the court's disposition, and in Class C cases the El Paso Municipal Court or Justice of the Peace file showing the deferred disposition and dismissal. Clients are sometimes surprised to learn a "dismissed" ticket was actually paid as a conviction, or that a warrant arrest years ago created a booking record they never knew about. That review is free.

If you qualify, we draft a verified petition for expunction and file it in an El Paso County district court. The petition must name every agency that may hold a record: the El Paso Police Department, the El Paso County Sheriff's Office, Texas DPS, the District or County Attorney, the City Attorney for municipal cases, the court clerk and any jail or magistrate that processed you. A missed agency keeps its copy, so the agency list gets real attention.

The court sets a hearing after the notice period the statute requires so the agencies can respond. For an eligible, well-documented petition, the hearing is often brief, and the judge signs the order. The clerk then sends certified copies to each agency, which must destroy the records. How long the whole process takes depends on the court's docket and the agencies' responses; timing cannot be promised.

sections.heading: Background Checks in a Fort Bliss and Border Economy
paragraphs: El Paso's job market runs on background checks. Fort Bliss contractors, federal positions, the ports of entry, hospitals, school districts and the trucking companies along I-10 all screen applicants, and many of those screens pull from the DPS database and from court records. A years-old driving while license invalid arrest or a dismissed Class C charge can show up as an "arrest record" with no disposition, which an HR reviewer reads as unresolved.

Security clearances and federal applications ask about arrests, not just convictions, and some federal forms have their own rules about expunged records. Before you submit one, we go over what you may and may not say on that specific form. For a state-level or private-employer check, an expunction generally means the honest answer is that there is nothing to disclose.

Private background-check vendors also scrape court data and keep stale copies. An expunction order gives you the legal basis to ask them to remove the record, and we provide the certified copy you need to do it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between expunction and nondisclosure in Texas?
faqs.a: Expunction orders the records destroyed and in general lets you deny the arrest; it is available mainly for dismissals, acquittals, no-bills and completed Class C deferrals. Nondisclosure seals the record from the public but keeps it visible to law enforcement and licensing agencies; it is the remedy for many completed deferred adjudications and certain convictions.

faqs.q: Can a traffic ticket be expunged in El Paso?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if the ticket was dismissed — including a dismissal after completed deferred disposition. A ticket you simply paid is a conviction and is generally not expungeable. We check the court's disposition first, because many people remember the outcome differently than the clerk recorded it.

faqs.q: How long does an expunction take in El Paso County?
faqs.a: It depends on the district court's docket and how quickly the agencies respond. The statute requires a notice period before the hearing, and after the order is signed the clerk mails certified copies to each agency for destruction of the records. Timing cannot be promised.

faqs.q: Do I have to go to court for the expunction hearing?
faqs.a: Often not. For an eligible, unopposed petition the hearing is brief and we appear for you. If an agency objects or the judge wants testimony, we will prepare you and attend together.

faqs.q: Is there a waiting period before I can file?
faqs.a: It depends on how the case ended. Dismissals after completed Class C deferred disposition are generally eligible once the dismissal is entered. Arrests that never resulted in a charge may require a waiting period based on the offense level. We confirm the applicable period under the current statute before filing.

faqs.q: What does an El Paso expunction cost?
faqs.a: We quote a flat fee after a free consultation, based on the number of arrests, courts and agencies involved. Filing fees and certified copies are set by the court and disclosed up front. Call 915-503-1600 or book a consultation online.
